OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Amodei to brief UNSC as France flags AI threat to kids, global security

Meeting called by Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot because AI's security implications had not received enough attention at the Security Council, says a French official.

Debdutta Chakraborty

23 September, 2026 03:54 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

France's President Emmanuel Macron addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, the US | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: France is convening a high-level meeting at the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) on Wednesday in which OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face CEOs will brief the 15-member council on the risks posed by artificial intelligence.

France holds the rotating presidency of the Security Council for September, coinciding with the opening of the 81st Session of the General Assembly in New York.

A French official said the meeting had been called by Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot because the security implications of artificial intelligence had not received enough attention at the Security Council.

Show Full Article

“We consider that artificial intelligence and the threat it could cause has not been sufficiently discussed, especially at the Security Council, and this is why Minister Barrault called for this meeting,” the official said at a media briefing.

French President Emmanuel Macron is expected to host an event focused on protecting children from potential harms associated with artificial intelligence. The initiative brings together governments, technology companies, civil society organisations and foundations, with the stated goal of ensuring that AI benefits children without harming their cognitive and social development.

About 20 countries are expected to participate at various levels, including heads of state and ministers, according to officials.

“The French president will have a major event on the protection of children with AI, which is a coalition bringing together governments, companies, civil society organisations, foundations, with a focus on ensuring that the development of AI benefits our children and do not harm their cognitive and social development, which is a key topic for the future of our society,” the French official added.

The Security Council meeting will address a different set of concerns. “AI has reached a level of development where it raises questions for global security,” the official said. “Now, on several fronts, the malicious use of models, but also the risk of losing control over advanced models, or autonomous weapons, for instance.”

The decision to invite the technology companies directly involved in developing advanced AI systems reflects the growing role of private companies in shaping the technology and its associated risks.

The official added that OpenAI was invited “in light of the recent security incident of this summer,” where independent AI test agents broke out of their sandboxes and accessed external systems, while Anthropic would appear “in light of its proposal on basing the development of advanced AI systems”.

According to the French officials, governments would ultimately have to establish the rules governing the technology and it will be discussed in the UNSC meeting.

The Security Council has previously addressed emerging technologies in the context of international peace and security, but the French initiative puts the rapidly evolving capabilities of generative and advanced AI systems directly before the council.

The first briefer will be Joshua Bengio, co-chair of the International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, who is expected to offer what the official described as “an independent academic perspective on the threats that AI causes to peace and security”.

He will be followed by Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, and Clément Delangue, the chief executive and co-founder of Hugging Face, the French artificial intelligence company.

Another French official said Paris believed the technology offered substantial benefits but also required international safeguards.

“First, by saying that France has put AI very firmly on the agenda of this UN General Assembly, and that was on purpose because AI is playing an increasingly important role around the world, no need to say about it,” the official added.

“We strongly believe in the immense benefits it could have, but it has to be done well.”

In the UN General Assembly’s 81st session Tuesday, France President Emmanuel Macron had also focused on the risks posed by AI, particularly the fact that most people and countries have little or no say in the debate over how the technology should be regulated.

He argued that decisions about AI should not be left solely to the US, China and a small group of private companies. The stakes, he said, were too high, given that the technology could threaten “the security of our States, of our hospitals, of our banks”.

“We must defend science. We have waited too long to protect our children and adolescents from social media. Everywhere in our societies, we see the consequences,” Macron said.

(Edited by Tony Rai)

Economic activity regains momentum in September after slump, survey shows

Indian economy proved more resilient than expected to a war-led energy shock, expanding 7.8% last quarter as household consumption & business investment-powered growth.

Anup Roy

23 September, 2026 01:10 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Market stalls in Mumbai, India. Photographer: Abeer Khan/Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

India’s economic activity accelerated in September, regaining momentum after slowing in recent months as manufacturing climbed to seven-month high and services picked up pace, a flash survey by HSBC Holdings Plc showed Wednesday.

The services purchasing managers’ index rose to 55.8 from 54.1 in August, while the manufacturing purchasing managers’ climbed rose to 55.7 from 52.8 last month. That left the composite index at 56.5, compared with 54.3 in August.

The indexes, which provide an early gauge of private-sector activity, are based on preliminary survey responses and may be revised when final PMI figures are released next month. A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while one below that level signals contraction.

Show Full Article

“Output growth ticked higher at both manufacturing and services companies, with goods producers leading the latest upturn. Aggregate new orders also rose at a quicker pace, prompting a solid expansion in jobs,” HSBC said in a statement. With the expansion in place, the composite index “was back above its long-run average,” it said.

Bond yields and rupee, however, stayed unchanged after the reading.

India’s economy proved more resilient than expected to a war-led energy shock, expanding 7.8% last quarter as household consumption and business investment powered growth. India, the world’s third-largest oil importer, remains vulnerable to elevated energy costs and supply disruptions that can weigh on domestic activity.

“Renewed tensions in the Middle East have once again led firms to build buffers to manage the uncertainties,” said Pranjul Bhandari, chief India economist at HSBC.

Brent crude is hovering around $100 a barrel. However, the government hasn’t raised pump prices since May, insulating the economy from volatile energy prices for now.

Still, price pressures are building. Figures last week showed India’s inflation accelerated in August, moving closer to the top of the central bank’s 2%-6% target range and potentially narrowing the scope for policymakers to remain on hold for long.

Most economists expect the Reserve Bank to raise interest rates on Oct. 7. The central bank has stayed on hold so far this year.

Trump meets Venezuela’s Delcy Rodriguez for the first time since Maduro’s capture

The meeting came during Rodriguez's first trip to the US since taking office. She is set to address the General Assembly Wednesday afternoon.

Reuters

23 September, 2026 09:43 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

FILE PHOTO: Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodriguez attends the signing of an agreement to re-establish relations with Paraguay, at Miraflores Palace in Caracas, Venezuela, September 19, 2026. REUTERS/Leonardo Fernandez Viloria/File Photo

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New York: US President Donald Trump met Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez late on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, their first meeting since American forces captured then-President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid.

The Venezuelan delegation, which includes the vice president of economy, the oil minister and officials from state oil company PDVSA, is focused on making the country look “investable,” two people close to the delegation told Reuters.

The pull-aside meeting during a reception Trump hosted during the UN General Assembly came during Rodriguez’s first trip to the US since taking office. She is set to address the General Assembly on Wednesday afternoon.

Show Full Article

A White House official said the meeting with Rodriguez included President Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, and Stephen Miller, assistant to the president and deputy chief of staff for policy.

Trump has built a working relationship with Rodriguez, who served as Maduro’s vice president. But critics say Washington has sidelined the opposition led by Maria Corina Machado, dropping demands for free elections in favor of oil and investment deals with the interim government. A small group of Venezuelans protested in New York on Tuesday, calling for elections.

In his speech to the General Assembly on Tuesday morning, Trump called Maduro an “outlaw dictator,” said hundreds of political prisoners had been freed since his capture and held up the raid as proof the US would use its “unmatched military might” to protect its interests in the Western Hemisphere.

“To the victor belong the spoils,” he said, calling an oil deal his administration signed with Caracas last month “perhaps the biggest deal ever made.” Trump has said he wants $100 billion in investment to flow into Venezuela’s oil industry.

Rodriguez arrived in New York on Monday with a delegation that has been holding talks on energy, mining and debt with US officials, multilateral lenders and companies, according to sources. The head of the Inter-American Development Bank is working to secure approval for a $2.5 billion loan for Venezuela but has faced pushback from some members of the lender’s board.

DEMONSTRATORS DEMAND FREE ELECTIONS

Earlier on Tuesday, more than 50 protesters gathered outside the UN to protest Rodriguez’s presence, waving Venezuelan flags and carrying signs reading “No Vote No Oil” and “New Face, Same Regime.” Many said they wanted Trump to push for free elections in the South American country.

The protesters sang the Venezuelan national anthem and chanted “Delcy, I swear, you’re going to Brooklyn with Maduro” — a reference to the federal jail in the New York City borough of Brooklyn, just across the East River from the UN, where her predecessor is being held pending trial on drug trafficking charges.

“On one hand, it’s outrageous to see part of the regime meeting with the authorities of this country’s current government, but there’s also no doubt that thanks to this government, today we are one step closer to freedom,” said Miguel Eduardo Martinez, a 34-year-old social media manager who moved from Caracas in 2017.

“Delcy Rodriguez wasn’t born on January 3, 2026. Delcy Rodriguez has been with the Chavista dictatorship for more than 20 years. She has been complicit,” said Cesar Coello, who carried a sign depicting Rodriguez in an orange jumpsuit.

Chavismo is the political movement founded by the late Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez.

Coello said he hoped Trump and Rodriguez would discuss holding elections soon.

(Reporting by Luc Cohen and Marianna Parraga in New York; Additional reporting by Gram Slattery, Writing by Nathan Crooks; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani and Stephen Coates)

Opinion

Kashmir brain drain is different from Kerala and Punjab

Data on money sent home by the Kashmiri diaspora remains poorly tracked. Kashmir loses its people for free, while other migrant-sending states in India at least get paid for theirs.

Tehmeena Rizvi

23 September, 2026 08:00 am IST

1

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

A flea market in Kashmir (Representational Image). | Photographer: Anindito Mukherjee | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

B eyond Kashmir’s security paradigm is a lived reality that most people won’t get to know. Kashmir’s youth migration is not a flight from militancy. It’s a simmering exodus that happens in two stages. Students first leave for degrees, then for jobs, and never return because those who migrate for specialised fields tend to settle wherever they land, while local university seats sit vacant behind them.

Educational vacancy is one part of it, another is the lack of big companies and expert fields. Even those who make it out often aren’t escaping, with many ending up underemployed outside the Valley — a lawyer outside law, an engineer in sales — trading local joblessness for outstation instability with no family safety net.

Though the same migration exists in other parts of India as well, Kashmir has built no remittance channel. It’s a measurable, worsening pattern, and it deserves to be read as an economic story, not just an emotional one.

Show Full Article

Jammu and Kashmir’s unemployment rate stood at 6.7 per cent as of early 2026, nearly double the national average of 3.5 per cent, according to figures the J&K government itself placed before the Assembly.

Among the 15-29 age group specifically, the picture is starker: 17.4 per cent unemployment against a national figure of 10.2 per cent for 2023-24, and in one quarter that year, nearly a third of young people in Kashmir’s urban areas were without work, the highest such figure recorded anywhere in the country.

More than 3.49 lakh youth are currently registered as unemployed with the Union Territory’s District Employment and Counselling Centres.

Over a lakh of them have postgraduate or graduate degrees. According to Kashmir’s own Economic Survey, the unemployment rate among educated youth is close to 46 per cent. This is probably an underestimate because registering with a government employment centre necessitates the kind of patience and paperwork that many young people, especially those who are already looking to move overseas, choose to forego.

Leaving the Valley often doesn’t guarantee a stable life for these young Kashmiris, with many struggling to make ends meet or ending up in jobs that don’t align with their skills and degrees. The situation looks more like that big American dream many cosmopolitan kids had in the 2000s.

Meanwhile, the outbound flow keeps growing, and local institutions are visibly emptying out because of it. By one widely cited estimate, about 30,000 students leave Jammu and Kashmir every year to study abroad, pursuing degrees in artificial intelligence, aerospace engineering, robotics, biomedical engineering, and other specialised fields that Kashmir’s own universities, for the most part, simply don’t offer. The trend has been going on for many years. And even today, if the universities in Kashmir have started offering such courses, they are not relevant to Kashmir’s job market.

At the University of Kashmir alone, hundreds of postgraduate seats have gone vacant in recent years. In 2023, about 124 postgraduate seats were left unfilled at the main Hazratbal campus alone, even as households in the Valley privately funded the same degrees in Delhi, Bengaluru, or abroad.

Two-staged migration What makes Kashmir’s version of migration distinct is that it happens in two stages, and each stage bleeds value out of the local economy in a different way.

The initial departure occurs at the point of higher education. In addition to taking their tuition costs with them, students who relocate to major cities in India or the UK also take with them the complete secondary economy that a student body produces, including rent, local expenditures, internships, and small businesses that are close to the college. In essence, Kashmir finances an education sector that it does not own, and the economic multiplier of that expenditure ends up in another city.

After graduation, the second exodus occurs, when these same students are unable to find employment in the area upon their return. The private sector in Kashmir is quite small. Historically, tourism, horticulture, and handicrafts have been the main drivers of the economy; these industries were designed for a different type of labour than what the area is currently providing. They don’t produce the white-collar, tech-related jobs that graduates in computer science or artificial intelligence are prepared for. Thus, graduates depart once more, initially to the cities of India and then gradually to the United States, the United Kingdom, and, primarily, the Gulf.

Here is where the comparison with other Indian states becomes genuinely instructive, and where Kashmir’s situation looks structurally different.

States like Kerala and Punjab have spent decades building formal channels for diaspora money to flow back through remittance corridors, NRI investment schemes, land and property markets explicitly built around returning or absentee earners, and even state government departments dedicated to diaspora affairs. Kerala’s economy, in particular, is substantially propped up by Gulf remittances that get counted, tracked, and reinvested locally through fairly mature financial infrastructure.

There is no similar channel in Kashmir. Money goes out for living expenses, tuition, application fees, and the years it takes to establish a life overseas, but nothing structured comes back. Institutions can carefully assess the increased security risks associated with these channels in order to provide room for innovation, or what we now refer to as the orange economy.

Data on money sent home by the Kashmiri diaspora remains poorly tracked, and that absence of data is itself a part of the story. It means that Kashmir loses its people for free, while other migrant-sending states in India at least get paid for theirs. The earnings that do return tend to arrive informally, through family transfers rather than structured investments, and rarely translate into local business formation the way they do in Kerala’s or Punjab’s diaspora economies.

This isn’t a static picture. Jammu and Kashmir’s Start-up Policy 2024-27 , incubators at NIT Srinagar, IIT Jammu, IIM Jammu, and IUST Awantipora, and a Software Technology Parks of India centre in Srinagar all represent a genuine, recent attempt to build local absorption capacity. Kashmir now counts over a thousand registered startups, and some Valley-based ventures have also pitched successfully on national platforms. Local delivery and logistics startups have created real, visible local jobs.

But registration numbers overstate the underlying reality. Few of these startups have scaled to the point where they can absorb the kind of specialised, foreign-trained talent that is leaving the Valley every year. A thousand registered startups is not the same as a thousand functioning employers, and the harder question here is : how many of these ventures actually pay salaries and survive past their second year ?

And this is not only about fields like AI or tech, this applies to fields like social sciences as well , particularly research, where we are yet to establish independent research expertise or institutions who work on real world problems or policy issues.

Also read: Srinagar’s cinemas may have gone dark. Kashmir’s love for films never did

What this actually costs The deeper cost of Kashmir’s youth migration isn’t simply the absence of a few thousand skilled workers. It’s the absence of the institutions, capital, and mentorship networks that returning skilled professionals typically build once critical mass is reached elsewhere; the kind of quiet compounding effect that turned Bengaluru into a tech hub or Kerala’s Gulf corridor into a functioning economic pillar.

Until Kashmir builds organisations capable of employing the graduates it produces and, equally, until it builds the financial and institutional channels to bring diaspora capital and expertise back in a trackable, reinvestable way, every departing flight from Srinagar will keep representing not just one student’s ambition, but a small, repeated transfer of the Valley’s future economic capacity to another city.

Tehmeena Rizvi, PhD, specialises in Women, Peace and Security studies in South Asia with a particular focus on Afghan Migration and the Kashmir region. She tweets @TehmeenaRizvi.  Views are personal.

(Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)
